source.text: הֵן־תֹּחַלְתּ֥וֹ נִכְזָ֑בָה הֲגַ֖ם אֶל־מַרְאָ֣יו יֻטָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, hope his is proved a lie; ? even at [the] sight of it is he hurled down?

en.L: Look, his hope is proved a lie; \q is he not hurled down even at the sight of it?
en.B: Any hope of overpowering it is false; \q the mere sight of it lays a person low.
en.R: No one can hope to defeat it. \q Just seeing it makes people fall down in fear.

decisions.choice: verse numbering: Hebrew 41:1-26 is 41:9-34 in many Bibles
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text, followed here, begins chapter 41 eight verses later than many Bibles do. So Hebrew 40:25-32 is numbered 41:1-8 there, and Hebrew 41:1-26 is numbered 41:9-34. The words are the same; only the numbers differ. Job is cited here by the Hebrew numbers.

decisions.choice: his hope: the hope of anyone who would try to capture Leviathan
decisions.reason: God is still speaking of Leviathan (40:25-32). "His" looks back to the one who would lay a hand on it (40:32): whoever hopes to master it will find the hope was a lie.

decisions.choice: a question expecting yes: even the sight of it throws a person down
alternatives: even a god is thrown down at the sight of it
decisions.reason: The question form "is he not ...?" makes a strong statement. The little word before "sight" is the preposition "at", as the text is pointed, not the word for God; so the line speaks of a human attacker who collapses before the fight begins.

decisions.choice: Any hope of overpowering it (B); No one can hope to defeat it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose hope is meant and what it is a hope for (m2), and turn the question into a plain statement (m3). Balanced says "a person", Readable "people", since anyone at all is meant.

source.text: לֹֽא־אַ֭כְזָר כִּ֣י יְעוּרֶ֑נּוּ וּמִ֥י ה֝֗וּא לְפָנַ֥י יִתְיַצָּֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: Not [is any one so] fierce that he will rouse it; and who [is] he [who] before me will take his stand?

en.L: No one [is so] fierce that he would rouse it; \q and who [is] he [who] will take his stand before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?
en.B: No one is fierce enough to stir it up; \q who then can stand up to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?
en.R: No one is brave enough to wake it up. \q So who could stand up against {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?

decisions.choice: rouse it: wake Leviathan
decisions.reason: The same verb is used in 3:8, where Job called on those "who are ready to rouse Leviathan" to curse his day. God now says that no one is bold enough to do it.

decisions.choice: an argument from the lesser to the greater: if no one dares face Leviathan, no one can stand before God
decisions.reason: Leviathan is only one of God's creatures (40:15, 19). If no human being dares to stir it up, much less can anyone take a stand against the God who made it, as Job has wanted to do in court (13:3, 18-22; 23:3-7).

decisions.choice: before me (the standard Hebrew text)
decisions.reason: The standard Hebrew text reads "before me", which gives the argument of m2. Some Hebrew manuscripts read "before it", which keeps the whole verse about Leviathan: who can stand up to it? The difference is one letter. The standard text is followed.

decisions.choice: brave enough (R)
decisions.reason: The word means fierce or cruel (30:21). Here it means bold enough to face danger, and Readable says that plainly.

source.text: מִ֣י הִ֭קְדִּימַנִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם תַּ֖חַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמַ֣יִם לִי־הֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: Who has come before me, and I will repay? Under all the heavens to me it [belongs].

en.L: Who has come before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, that I should repay [him]? \q Under all the heavens, it [is] {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}.
en.B: Who has first given to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, that I should pay {{gender:them|him}} back? \q Everything under the whole heaven is {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}.
en.R: Who has ever given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} anything that I must pay back? \q Everything under heaven belongs to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: has come before me ... that I should repay: has given to God first, so that God is in debt
alternatives: has confronted me, and I will repay (punish) him
who has confronted it and come out unharmed?
decisions.reason: The verb means to come to meet someone or to go before them. Followed by "repay", it pictures someone who has done God a favor first and can now demand payment. Paul quotes the thought in this sense in Romans 11:35. Others read it as a challenge, "Who has confronted me?" With different vowels the line can also be read as being about Leviathan: "Who has confronted it and remained safe?" The standard text and the sense of debt are followed.

decisions.choice: God owes no one anything, because everything is already his
decisions.reason: Under all the heavens everything belongs to God (Psalm 50:12; Deuteronomy 10:14). Job has demanded that God answer to him as to a creditor in court; God replies that no creature can put him in its debt.

decisions.choice: first given to me (B); ever given me anything (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "coming before" God means here (m1). The person repaid is anyone at all, so Balanced uses the gender setting.

source.text: לֽוֹ־אַחֲרִ֥ישׁ בַּדָּ֑יו וּדְבַר־גְּ֝בוּר֗וֹת וְחִ֣ין עֶרְכּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Concerning it [written: not] I will keep silent, limbs its, and [the] matter of mighty deeds and [the] grace of frame its.

en.L: I will not keep silent about its limbs, \q or the account of its might, and the grace of its frame.
en.B: I will not keep silent about its limbs, \q its mighty strength and its fine build.
en.R: I will tell you about its body, \q about its great strength and how well it is made.

decisions.choice: written "not", read "concerning it"
alternatives: I will not keep silent (as written)
concerning it I will keep silent no longer (as read)
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell "not"; the scribes' reading note gives the same sounds as "to it" or "concerning it", which the word data here follows. Either way the line announces that God will now speak about Leviathan's body, which the following verses do. The sense "I will not keep silent" is given at every level.

decisions.choice: its limbs: the parts of its body
decisions.reason: The word means limbs or parts of the body (18:13). God turns from what no one can do to Leviathan (40:25-41:3) to a description of its body, from its hide and jaws to its underside (41:5-22).

decisions.choice: the grace of its frame: the beauty and fitness of the way it is built
decisions.reason: The word for "frame" means an arrangement or order, and the word before it, a rare form, is taken to mean grace or beauty. Some read the letters as "there is none like its frame". God admires the creature he made.

decisions.choice: I will tell you about (R)
alternatives: I will not keep silent about
decisions.reason: Readable says positively what the double negative means: God will now speak about the creature.

source.text: מִֽי־גִ֭לָּה פְּנֵ֣י לְבוּשׁ֑וֹ בְּכֶ֥פֶל רִ֝סְנ֗וֹ מִ֣י יָבֽוֹא׃

records.literal_gloss: Who has uncovered [the] face of garment its? Into [the] double of bridle its who will come?

en.L: Who has stripped off the face of its garment? \q Into its double bridle who can come?
en.B: Who can strip off its outer coat? \q Who can come at it with a double bridle?
en.R: Who can strip off its tough hide? \q Who can get close enough to put a bridle on it?

decisions.choice: the face of its garment: its outer covering, the hide and scales
decisions.reason: The "garment" is Leviathan's skin with its armor of scales (41:7-9); its "face" is the outside. No hunter can skin it.

decisions.choice: its double bridle: a bridle for its huge jaws
decisions.reason: The word means a bridle or halter (30:11; Isaiah 30:28), and "double" may describe the two jaws where a bridle would go, or its double row of teeth (41:6). With one letter different the word would mean a coat of mail, giving "Who can get through its double armor?" The standard text is followed. Either way no one can tame or pierce the creature.

decisions.choice: Who can ... (B, R)
decisions.reason: The question is about what anyone could do, not about a past event; Balanced and Readable say "Who can". Readable says "tough hide" for the garment picture (m1).

source.text: דַּלְתֵ֣י פָ֭נָיו מִ֣י פִתֵּ֑חַ סְבִיב֖וֹת שִׁנָּ֣יו אֵימָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] doors of face its who has opened? Around teeth its [is] terror.

en.L: The doors of its face, who has opened [them]? \q All around its teeth [is] terror.
en.B: Who can pry open the doors of its face? \q Its teeth all around are a terror.
en.R: Who can force its jaws open? \q Its teeth are terrifying.

decisions.choice: the doors of its face: its jaws
decisions.reason: Its jaws are pictured as the double doors of a gate. No one can open them, as no one could open Leviathan's mouth with a hook (40:25-26).

decisions.choice: around its teeth is terror: the rows of teeth strike terror
decisions.reason: The line is a statement without a verb: the teeth all round its mouth are terror itself to anyone who sees them.

decisions.choice: its jaws (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means (m1); Literal and Balanced keep the doors.

source.text: גַּ֭אֲוָה אֲפִיקֵ֣י מָֽגִנִּ֑ים סָ֝ג֗וּר חוֹתָ֥ם צָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Pride [are] rows of shields, shut up [with] a seal tight.

en.L: [Its] pride [is the] rows of shields, \q shut up [with] a tight seal.
en.B: Its pride is its rows of shields, \q shut together as with a tight seal.
en.R: It is proud of its scales, like rows of shields \q closed up tight as if sealed.

decisions.choice: pride (the standard Hebrew text)
alternatives: its back (the same letters with different vowels)
decisions.reason: The standard text has "pride": the creature's pride and glory are its scales. With different vowels the same letters can be read "its back", giving "Its back is rows of shields". The standard text is followed; pride is also where the description ends (41:26).

decisions.choice: rows of shields: its scales, set in rows like the shields of soldiers
decisions.reason: The first word usually means channels or streams; here it is taken to mean rows. The shields are the scales of its hide, set side by side and too hard to pierce (41:18-21).

decisions.choice: shut up with a tight seal: fitted together so closely that nothing gets through
decisions.reason: A seal closed a jar or a document so that nothing could open it. The scales are joined as if sealed shut; verses 8-9 say the same thing again.

decisions.choice: its scales, like rows of shields (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the scales and keeps the picture of shields as a comparison (m2).

source.text: אֶחָ֣ד בְּאֶחָ֣ד יִגַּ֑שׁוּ וְ֝ר֗וּחַ לֹא־יָב֥וֹא בֵֽינֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: One to one they draw near, and air not comes between them.

en.L: One to one they draw near, \q and air does not come between them.
en.B: Each one is so close to the next \q that no air can pass between them.
en.R: They fit so close together \q that not even air can get between them.

decisions.choice: air: a breath of air
decisions.reason: The word (ruach) can mean wind, breath or spirit. Here it is the smallest breath of air, which cannot slip between the scales.

decisions.choice: so close ... that
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the two lines side by side; Balanced and Readable say how they are related: the scales are so close that no air passes.

source.text: אִישׁ־בְּאָחִ֥יהוּ יְדֻבָּ֑קוּ יִ֝תְלַכְּד֗וּ וְלֹ֣א יִתְפָּרָֽדוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Each to brother its they are joined; they grip one another and not are separated.

en.L: Each to its brother they are joined; \q they grip one another and are not separated.
en.B: They are joined one to another; \q they cling together and cannot be pulled apart.
en.R: They are locked together; \q they hold on to each other, and nothing can separate them.

decisions.choice: each to its brother: each one to the next
decisions.reason: "A man to his brother" is the Hebrew way of saying "one to another", used even of things (Exodus 25:20, of the cherubim's faces). The scales are meant.

decisions.choice: are not separated: cannot be pulled apart
decisions.reason: The verb form describes what never happens, and so what cannot happen: nothing pries the scales apart.

decisions.choice: one to another (B); locked together (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m1); Literal keeps it.

source.text: עֲֽ֭טִישֹׁתָיו תָּ֣הֶל א֑וֹר וְ֝עֵינָ֗יו כְּעַפְעַפֵּי־שָֽׁחַר׃

records.literal_gloss: Sneezings its flash forth light, and eyes its [are] like [the] eyelids of dawn.

en.L: Its sneezings flash forth light, \q and its eyes [are] like the eyelids of dawn.
en.B: Its snorting makes light flash out, \q and its eyes are like the first rays of dawn.
en.R: When it snorts, light flashes out. \q Its eyes glow like the sunrise.

decisions.choice: its sneezings flash forth light: the spray it snorts out shines
decisions.reason: The word means a sneeze, the only time it is used in the Bible. When the great creature blows spray from its nostrils, the mist flashes in the light.

decisions.choice: the eyelids of dawn: the first light of morning
decisions.reason: The same phrase is in 3:9, where Job wished that the night of his birth would never "see the eyelids of dawn". The opening light of morning is pictured as an eye opening; Leviathan's eyes shine like it.

decisions.choice: snorting (B, R); the first rays of dawn (B); the sunrise (R)
decisions.reason: "Sneezing" sounds comic in English, so Balanced and Readable say "snorting". They give the meaning of "the eyelids of dawn" (m2), which Literal keeps.

source.text: מִ֭פִּיו לַפִּידִ֣ים יַהֲלֹ֑כוּ כִּיד֥וֹדֵי אֵ֝֗שׁ יִתְמַלָּֽטוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: From mouth its torches go; sparks of fire escape.

en.L: From its mouth go torches; \q sparks of fire leap out.
en.B: Flaming torches pour from its mouth; \q sparks of fire shoot out.
en.R: Fire comes out of its mouth like torches, \q and sparks fly out.

decisions.choice: torches go from its mouth: a poetic picture of its fiery breath
decisions.reason: Verses 10-13 picture the creature as breathing light, smoke and fire. The poem uses the language of the great sea monster of the old poems (3:8; Psalm 74:14), larger and more terrible than any animal people hunt, to show what God alone can master.

decisions.choice: sparks: flying sparks
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here. It is related to a word for striking out sparks, and the line beside it with "fire" makes the sense clear.

decisions.choice: Fire comes out ... like torches (R)
decisions.reason: Readable turns the picture into a comparison so that it is clear that fire, not torches, comes from its mouth.

source.text: מִ֭נְּחִירָיו יֵצֵ֣א עָשָׁ֑ן כְּד֖וּד נָפ֣וּחַ וְאַגְמֹֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: From nostrils its goes out smoke, as [from] a pot blown upon and rushes.

en.L: From its nostrils goes out smoke, \q as [from] a pot blown upon, and rushes.
en.B: Smoke pours from its nostrils \q as from a pot fanned to a boil over burning reeds.
en.R: Smoke comes out of its nose, \q like steam from a pot boiling over a fire of reeds.

decisions.choice: a pot blown upon: a pot over a fire that is fanned until it boils
decisions.reason: The word means a cooking pot or basket (1 Samuel 2:14; Jeremiah 24:2). "Blown upon" describes the fire under it, fanned to make it burn hot (compare Jeremiah 1:13, "a boiling pot", the same word for "blown").

decisions.choice: rushes: reeds burning as fuel under the pot
decisions.reason: The word means a bulrush or reed (40:26, where a cord made of rushes is meant). How it joins the line is not clear: most likely the reeds are the fuel, burning with smoke under the pot. Some take it as a separate picture of a smoking reed.

decisions.choice: fanned to a boil over burning reeds (B); boiling over a fire of reeds (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how the pot and the rushes belong together (m1, m2).

source.text: נַ֭פְשׁוֹ גֶּחָלִ֣ים תְּלַהֵ֑ט וְ֝לַ֗הַב מִפִּ֥יו יֵצֵֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Breath its coals sets ablaze, and a flame from mouth its goes out.

en.L: Its breath sets coals ablaze, \q and a flame goes out from its mouth.
en.B: Its breath sets coals on fire, \q and flames dart from its mouth.
en.R: Its breath can set coals on fire, \q and flames shoot out of its mouth.

decisions.choice: its breath
decisions.reason: The word (nefesh) often means life or self, but its first meaning is throat or breath, which fits here beside "mouth".

decisions.choice: smoke and fire from mouth and nostrils
decisions.reason: Psalm 18:9 uses the same pictures of God coming in anger: smoke went up from his nostrils, fire from his mouth, coals blazed. The terror that people feel before Leviathan is a small likeness of the terror of God (41:2).

source.text: בְּֽ֭צַוָּארוֹ יָלִ֣ין עֹ֑ז וּ֝לְפָנָ֗יו תָּד֥וּץ דְּאָבָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: In neck its lodges strength, and before it dances dismay.

en.L: In its neck lodges strength, \q and before it dismay dances.
en.B: Strength makes its home in its neck, \q and terror dances before it.
en.R: Its neck is full of strength, \q and fear runs ahead of it wherever it goes.

decisions.choice: strength lodges in its neck: its neck is where its power lives
decisions.reason: The verb means to spend the night or to stay. Strength is pictured as a guest who has made its home in the creature's neck and never leaves.

decisions.choice: dismay dances before it: terror goes ahead of it
decisions.reason: The noun, used only here, means dismay or faintness of heart. It is pictured as a person leaping along in front of the creature: wherever it comes, terror arrives first.

decisions.choice: fear runs ahead of it wherever it goes (R)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the picture (m2) in plain words.

source.text: מַפְּלֵ֣י בְשָׂר֣וֹ דָבֵ֑קוּ יָצ֥וּק עָ֝לָ֗יו בַּל־יִמּֽוֹט׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] folds of flesh its cling together; [it is] cast on it, not it is moved.

en.L: The folds of its flesh cling together; \q [they are] cast firm on it, it is not moved.
en.B: The folds of its flesh are tightly joined; \q they are set firm on it and do not move.
en.R: The folds of its skin are joined tightly. \q They are as hard as metal and cannot be moved.

decisions.choice: the folds of its flesh: the loose-hanging parts of its body
decisions.reason: The first word comes from a verb meaning to fall or hang down; here it is the flesh that would hang loose on other animals, under the belly and neck. On Leviathan even these are firm.

decisions.choice: cast: firm as metal poured in a mold
decisions.reason: The word means poured out, and so cast, like metal set hard in a mold (37:18, of the sky "hard as a cast mirror"; 38:38). It is used three times in verses 15-16 to stress how hard the creature is.

decisions.choice: as hard as metal (R)
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of cast metal (m2).

source.text: לִ֭בּוֹ יָצ֣וּק כְּמוֹ־אָ֑בֶן וְ֝יָצ֗וּק כְּפֶ֣לַח תַּחְתִּֽית׃

records.literal_gloss: Heart its [is] cast like a stone, and cast like a millstone lower.

en.L: Its heart [is] cast like a stone, \q and cast like a lower millstone.
en.B: Its heart is as hard as rock, \q as hard as a lower millstone.
en.R: Its heart is as hard as rock, \q as hard as the bottom stone of a mill.

decisions.choice: its heart: its chest, and with it its courage
decisions.reason: The heart can mean the inner body or the inner person. Here both are meant: its chest is hard as stone, and nothing can frighten it (41:25).

decisions.choice: a lower millstone: the bottom stone of a hand mill
decisions.reason: Grain was ground between two stones. The lower one bore all the weight and pounding of the upper stone, so it had to be the hardest.

decisions.choice: the bottom stone of a mill (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what a lower millstone is (m2).

source.text: מִ֭שֵּׂתוֹ יָג֣וּרוּ אֵלִ֑ים מִ֝שְּׁבָרִ֗ים יִתְחַטָּֽאוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: From rising up its are afraid [the] mighty; from crashings they are bewildered.

en.L: At its rising up the mighty are afraid; \q at the crashing they are beside themselves.
en.B: When it raises itself up, the mighty are afraid; \q at its crashing they are thrown into confusion.
en.R: When it rises up, even the strongest are afraid. \q When it crashes about, they do not know where to turn.

decisions.choice: the mighty: the strongest of men
decisions.reason: The word can mean mighty men (Exodus 15:15; Ezekiel 17:13) or gods (Exodus 15:11). If "gods" is meant, the verse says that even divine beings fear Leviathan, as in the old poems. The first sense is followed; either way no one stands before it.

decisions.choice: crashings: the crash of its thrashing, or of the waves it raises
decisions.reason: The word means breaking or crashing, and is used of breakers in the sea (Psalm 42:8 has a related word). It is the crash when the creature thrashes and the water breaks around it.

decisions.choice: they are beside themselves: they lose their way in panic
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the root meaning to miss the mark. Here it means that people are thrown off course and do not know what to do.

decisions.choice: they do not know where to turn (R)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the verb (m3) in plain words.

source.text: מַשִּׂיגֵ֣הוּ חֶ֭רֶב בְּלִ֣י תָק֑וּם חֲנִ֖ית מַסָּ֣ע וְשִׁרְיָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] reaching it [with] a sword not it holds, spear, dart, and javelin.

en.L: [If one] reaches it [with] a sword, it does not hold, \q [nor] spear, dart, or javelin.
en.B: A sword that reaches it has no effect, \q nor does a spear, a dart, or a javelin.
en.R: A sword cannot hurt it, \q and neither can a spear, a dart, or a javelin.

decisions.choice: a sword that reaches it does not hold
decisions.reason: The line begins with "one reaching it". Even when a sword gets close enough to strike, it does not stand up against the creature; it has no effect (compare 41:19-21).

decisions.choice: dart, javelin: kinds of thrown weapons
alternatives: coat of mail (for the last word)
decisions.reason: Both words are rare, and the exact weapons are not known. Some link the last word to the word for a coat of mail, but in a list of weapons it is most likely a kind of javelin.

decisions.choice: has no effect (B); cannot hurt it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what it means for the sword not to "hold" (m1).

source.text: יַחְשֹׁ֣ב לְתֶ֣בֶן בַּרְזֶ֑ל לְעֵ֖ץ רִקָּב֣וֹן נְחוּשָֽׁה׃

records.literal_gloss: It considers as straw iron, as wood of rottenness bronze.

en.L: It regards iron as straw, \q bronze as rotten wood.
en.B: It treats iron like straw \q and bronze like rotten wood.
en.R: To it, iron is like straw, \q and bronze is like rotten wood.

decisions.choice: iron and bronze: the metals of weapons and armor
decisions.reason: Iron and bronze were the hardest materials known for weapons and armor (20:24, "the iron weapon" and "the bronze bow"). Leviathan treats the strongest things people can make as weak and worthless.

source.text: לֹֽא־יַבְרִיחֶ֥נּוּ בֶן־קָ֑שֶׁת לְ֝קַ֗שׁ נֶהְפְּכוּ־ל֥וֹ אַבְנֵי־קָֽלַע׃

records.literal_gloss: Not makes flee it [the] son of a bow; into chaff are turned for it [the] stones of a sling.

en.L: The son of a bow does not make it flee; \q sling stones are turned into chaff for it.
en.B: Arrows do not make it run away; \q sling stones are like chaff to it.
en.R: Arrows cannot make it run away. \q Stones from a sling are like bits of straw to it.

decisions.choice: the son of a bow: an arrow
decisions.reason: Hebrew often calls something the "son" of what it comes from; an arrow is the "son" of the bow (compare Lamentations 3:13, "the sons of his quiver").

decisions.choice: chaff: dry stubble or straw that is worthless and light
decisions.reason: The word means dry stubble or chaff, which the wind blows away (13:25; Psalm 83:14). The stones do it no more harm than chaff would.

decisions.choice: arrows (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m1).

source.text: כְּ֭קַשׁ נֶחְשְׁב֣וּ תוֹתָ֑ח וְ֝יִשְׂחַ֗ק לְרַ֣עַשׁ כִּידֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Like chaff are regarded clubs; and it laughs at [the] rattling of a javelin.

en.L: Like chaff a club is regarded, \q and it laughs at the rattling of a javelin.
en.B: A club seems like chaff to it, \q and it laughs at the rattle of a javelin.
en.R: Clubs are like straw to it. \q It laughs when a spear comes rattling toward it.

decisions.choice: a club: a heavy war club
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here; most likely it is a heavy club or mace. The verb with it is plural, so it may mean clubs of every kind.

decisions.choice: the rattling of a javelin: the whirr and shaking of a javelin thrown at it
decisions.reason: The javelin is the weapon that rattles against the warhorse in 39:23. The noise of battle does not trouble Leviathan.

decisions.choice: it laughs: it scorns what would frighten others
decisions.reason: The wild donkey laughs at the noise of the city (39:7), the ostrich at the horse and rider (39:18), and the warhorse at fear (39:22). Leviathan laughs at the weapons of war.

source.text: תַּ֭חְתָּיו חַדּ֣וּדֵי חָ֑רֶשׂ יִרְפַּ֖ד חָר֣וּץ עֲלֵי־טִֽיט׃

records.literal_gloss: Under it [are] sharp points of potsherd; it spreads out a threshing sledge on [the] mud.

en.L: Under it [are] sharp points of potsherd; \q it spreads out a threshing sledge on the mud.
en.B: Its underside is like jagged pieces of pottery; \q it leaves a trail in the mud like a threshing sledge.
en.R: Its belly is as sharp as broken pottery. \q It leaves marks in the mud like a threshing sledge.

decisions.choice: sharp points of potsherd: its underside is as rough and sharp as broken pottery
decisions.reason: A potsherd is a piece of broken pottery, with sharp edges (2:8, where Job scraped himself with one). The scales under its belly are like them.

decisions.choice: a threshing sledge: a heavy board with sharp stones or iron set underneath
decisions.reason: Grain was threshed by dragging a heavy wooden sledge over it; sharp stones or iron teeth under the board cut the stalks (Isaiah 41:15; Amos 1:3). Where Leviathan crawls through the mud, it leaves marks like such a sledge.

decisions.choice: it leaves a trail (B) / marks (R) in the mud like a threshing sledge
alternatives: it spreads out a threshing sledge
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the picture into a comparison and say what it leaves behind.

source.text: יַרְתִּ֣יחַ כַּסִּ֣יר מְצוּלָ֑ה יָ֝֗ם יָשִׂ֥ים כַּמֶּרְקָחָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: It makes boil like the pot [the] deep; [the] sea it makes like the pot of ointment.

en.L: It makes the deep boil like a pot; \q it makes the sea like a pot of ointment.
en.B: It makes the depths churn like a boiling pot; \q it stirs up the sea like a pot of perfumed oil.
en.R: It makes the deep water boil like a pot. \q It stirs up the sea like oil being mixed in a pot.

decisions.choice: a pot of ointment: a pot where perfumed oil is mixed and heated
decisions.reason: Perfumed oil was made by heating oil with spices and stirring it (Exodus 30:25). The foaming sea is like the bubbling oil in such a pot.

decisions.choice: the deep, the sea: the waters where Leviathan lives
decisions.reason: The first word means the depths of the sea (Jonah 2:4; Psalm 107:24). Leviathan is the creature of the sea, which God made it to play in (Psalm 104:26).

source.text: אַ֭חֲרָיו יָאִ֣יר נָתִ֑יב יַחְשֹׁ֖ב תְּה֣וֹם לְשֵׂיבָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Behind it it makes shine a path; one considers [the] deep to [be] gray hair.

en.L: Behind it it makes a path shine; \q one would think the deep [had] gray hair.
en.B: It leaves a shining wake behind it; \q one would think the deep had white hair.
en.R: It leaves a bright trail behind it in the water. \q You would think the deep sea had white hair.

decisions.choice: the deep had gray hair: its wake is white with foam
decisions.reason: The white foam of the wake is pictured as the white hair of an old man. The "deep" (tehom) is the great ocean (38:16, 30; Genesis 1:2).

decisions.choice: white hair (B, R)
decisions.reason: The word means the gray or white hair of old age (15:10). In English "white hair" better fits the white of foam.

source.text: אֵֽין־עַל־עָפָ֥ר מָשְׁל֑וֹ הֶ֝עָשׂ֗וּ לִבְלִי־חָֽת׃

records.literal_gloss: There is not on [the] dust likeness its, the [one] made for being without terror.

en.L: There is not on [the] dust its like, \q the [one] made to be without fear.
en.B: Nothing on earth is its equal, \q a creature made without fear.
en.R: There is nothing like it on earth. \q It was made to have no fear.

decisions.choice: the dust: the earth, the dry land
decisions.reason: "Dust" stands for the earth and its ground (19:25; 30:6). Nothing on the earth compares with this creature of the sea.

decisions.choice: the one made: a creature that God made
decisions.reason: However terrible it is, Leviathan was made, as Behemoth was made by God alongside Job (40:15, 19). Psalm 104:26 says God formed Leviathan to play in the sea.

decisions.choice: without fear: it knows no terror
decisions.reason: The noun means terror or dread (compare 41:17, where the mighty are afraid of it). It fears nothing, while everything else fears it.

source.text: אֵֽת־כָּל־גָּבֹ֥הַּ יִרְאֶ֑ה ה֝֗וּא מֶ֣לֶךְ עַל־כָּל־בְּנֵי־שָֽׁחַץ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Every high [thing] it looks on; it [is] king over all [the] sons of pride.

en.L: Every high [thing] it looks on; \q it [is] king over all the sons of pride.
en.B: It looks down on everything that is lofty; \q it is king over all the proud beasts.
en.R: It looks down on everything that is high and mighty. \q It is king over every proud creature.

decisions.choice: the sons of pride: the proud wild beasts
decisions.reason: The same phrase in 28:8 means the proud wild beasts, which have not walked the hidden paths of the mines. Leviathan is the greatest of them all.

decisions.choice: it looks on every high thing: what God asked Job to do
decisions.reason: In 40:11-12 God challenged Job to look on everyone who is proud and bring him low. Job cannot do it, but Leviathan looks down on everything high, and God is master of Leviathan. With this verse God's speeches end; Job answers in 42:1-6.

decisions.choice: the proud beasts (B); every proud creature (R)
decisions.reason: As in 28:8, Balanced and Readable say who the "sons of pride" are (m1).
